newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels shoot down chopper, 24 dead.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels shoot down chopper, 24 dead.

text.p: Leftist rebels shot down an army helicopter over rugged terrain in an oil-rich region of eastern Colombia on Sunday, killing at least 21 soldiers and three civilians, military sources said.

The Russian-made Mi-17 chopper, contracted out by a civilian aviation company, was flying to a remote area in Arauca province after National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels dynamited a section of Colombia's largest oil pipeline earlier in the day, an army spokeswoman said.
The pipeline serves the Cano Limon field operated by U.S. multinational Occidental Petroleum Corp.

"The helicopter was shot at by narco-bandits and came down. It blew up as it hit the ground and unfortunately none of the soldiers managed to get out," Col. Roberto Trujillo, of the army's Second Brigade, told the Radionet radio network.
"All the people on board have died unless by some miracle somebody managed to get out but I think that would have been very difficult," he added.
He said one officer, two junior officers, 18 soldiers and three civilian crew members were on board the helicopter went it was shot down near the town of Arauquita.

An army spokeswoman told Reuters that the attack was carried out Sunday by a group of about 30 guerrillas of the ELN, Colombia's second largest rebel army which was set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966 and specializes in attacks on the country's key oil infrastructure.

Trujillo said he did not know what weapons the rebels had used to shoot down the helicopter but said air and ground troops had been sent to the area, believed to be heavily mined, to recover the dead.

The helicopter had been on its way to assess damage following an ELN attack some two hours earlier on the oil pipeline, which runs from Occidental's Cano Limon field to the Caribbean coast oil terminal at Covenas and pumps about 200,000 barrels of crude per day.

It was the 36th time this year the pipeline has been blown up, a spokesman for the state-run oil company Ecopetrol told Reuters. He said it was too early to say how much crude was spilled in the blast, which brought pumping operations to a standstill.
Both army top brass and defense experts have frequently condemned the military's use of Mi-17 helicopters for troop movements over areas where rebels operate.
